summary: Describes a situation in which the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), the routing protocol between autonomous systems, can fall into a persistent route oscillation that never settles. It explains the conditions that cause this behavior.

plainLanguage.summary: Some BGP network designs let routers see different sets of routes. When routers compare MED values using those partial views, their best-route choices can keep changing without settling.

subtitle: How route reflection or confederations and MED can cause BGP paths to oscillate.

tldr.problem: BGP route reflection and AS confederations can hide some exit paths, and MED comparisons can make routers repeatedly change their best route.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines Type I and Type II persistent route oscillation, gives examples, and lists network-design workarounds.
tldr.outcome: The behavior is deterministic and can be avoided by design choices, but the authors say protocol enhancements are needed for a long-term solution.

today: RFC 3345 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo records the oscillation problem and calls for protocol enhancements.

sections.title: How Partial Route Visibility Causes Oscillation
sections.content:
BGP exchanges reachability information between autonomous systems. Route reflection and AS confederations reduce the need for a full internal BGP mesh, but they can leave routers with partial and inconsistent views of exit paths.

BGP compares the MULTI_EXIT_DISC (MED) attribute only between routes learned from the same neighboring AS. In certain network designs, local route choices based on different visible paths can conflict and create persistent oscillation.
sections.plainLanguage: Route reflection and confederations reduce the number of internal BGP connections, but routers may see different paths. Their different views can make best-route choices change repeatedly.

sections.title: Type I Churn
sections.content:
Type I churn requires a single-level route-reflection or confederation design and MED values from two or more ASs for one prefix, with unique values. The RFC shows both a route-reflection example and a confederation example.

In the route-reflection example, one router selects a route using IGP cost, another changes its selection based on a lower MED, and the resulting advertisements cause the first router to return to its earlier choice. The sequence then repeats.
sections.plainLanguage: Type I needs a single-level reflection or confederation design and distinct MED values from multiple ASs. Routers can then repeatedly change which route they select.

sections.title: Type II Churn
sections.content:
Type II churn requires more than one tier of route reflection or Sub-ASs, together with MED values from two or more ASs for one prefix that are unique. The memo illustrates this type using a confederation.

In the example, routers compare IGP costs and MED values as route updates arrive. The RFC traces eight steps before the routing tables return to an earlier point and repeat the cycle.
sections.plainLanguage: Type II involves multiple tiers of route reflection or Sub-ASs as well as distinct MED values from multiple ASs. The example returns to an earlier route state after eight steps.

sections.title: Workarounds for the Two Types
sections.content:
For Type I, the preferred route-reflection workaround is to give inter-cluster links a higher IGP metric than intra-cluster links. For confederations, the memo recommends the same relationship between inter-Sub-AS and intra-Sub-AS links.

Other possibilities include not accepting MED, selecting routes using higher-priority attributes, comparing MED across ASs, or using a full iBGP mesh. For Type II, the memo also suggests avoiding multiple tiers or meshing clients or border routers. It cautions that several options may be impractical.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo recommends making inter-cluster or inter-Sub-AS links cost more than internal links for Type I. Other workarounds change how MED is used or how routers share routes.

sections.title: Protocol Work and Security Note
sections.content:
The authors say protocol enhancements must be pursued because network-design requirements are not a reasonable long-term fix. They say this problem should not occur under default protocol configurations.

The Security Considerations section states that the discussion introduces no new security concerns to BGP or the referenced specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say the protocol should be improved so operators do not need lasting design workarounds. They identify no new security concerns.
